subject: Cognitive Science
title: Babbling and First Words
description: A short lesson to help you apply Babbling and First Words.

hook.text: At six months a baby babbles "ba-ba-ba." By twelve months "ba-ba" becomes "ball." Meaning arrives.

buildup.text: Babbling follows a universal sequence: cooing at two months, canonical babbling by six months.

discovery.text: Even deaf babies babble—with their hands. Sign-exposed children produce manual babbling on time.

twist.text: First words are mostly nouns for objects kids can act on. "Ball" appears across nearly every language.

climax.text: Around eighteen months, the vocabulary explosion hits. Children learn up to ten words per day.

punchline.text: From babble to words in twelve months flat.

quiz.question: What do deaf babies do instead of vocal babbling?

details.summary: Babies begin babbling around six months, producing syllables like ba-ba and da-da that gradually narrow to the sounds of their native language. First words appear around twelve months.
details.whyItMatters: Babbling is not random noise but a crucial rehearsal for speech. It shows how the brain prunes unused sound categories and strengthens the ones that matter locally.
takeaways: Babbling begins around six months with universal syllables
Sound repertoire narrows to native language patterns
First meaningful words typically appear around 12 months

faq.question: Do deaf babies babble differently?
faq.answer: Deaf babies begin vocal babbling slightly later and with less variety, but those exposed to sign language produce manual babbling, rhythmic hand movements that mirror vocal babbling patterns. This suggests babbling is a universal motor rehearsal for whatever language modality is available.

faq.question: Why do babies lose the ability to hear all sounds?
faq.answer: Perceptual narrowing improves efficiency. By focusing on sounds that matter in their language, babies become experts at distinguishing meaningful differences. Japanese infants lose the ability to distinguish R and L around 10 months because this distinction is irrelevant in Japanese.
